content: The Surveillance Guide for Vaccine-Preventable Diseases in the WHO South-East Asia Region: Pertussis (Module 5, September 2023) is a comprehensive document published by the World Health Organization (WHO). It provides detailed guidance on the surveillance, diagnosis, and management of pertussis (whooping cough) in the South-East Asia region. Introduction to Pertussis Surveillance The high transmission rates of pertussis in several countries highlight the waning immunity provided by acellular pertussis vaccines, necessitating additional booster doses for better disease control. Low-income countries using whole-cell pertussis vaccines lack sufficient epidemiological data, which is critical for formulating policies on booster doses. Surveillance is essential to monitor the disease burden, assess the impact of vaccination programs, and guide public health responses to outbreaks. Objectives of Pertussis Surveillance 1. Monitor Disease Burden: Focus on morbidity and mortality, particularly in children under five years of age. 2. Generate Data for Vaccine Policy: Inform decisions on vaccine schedules and delivery strategies to optimize vaccination impact. 3. Guide Public Health Responses: Provide data to manage and respond to pertussis outbreaks effectively. Case Detection and Definition A suspected case is defined as: A person of any age with a cough lasting ≥2 weeks, or any duration in infants or outbreak settings, without a more likely diagnosis, and at least one of the following symptoms: Paroxysms (fits) of coughing. Inspiratory whooping. Post-tussive vomiting (vomiting after coughing) without other apparent causes. Apnea (in infants under one year of age). Physicians may suspect pertussis in patients with a cough of any duration. Immunized or previously infected individuals may present atypically, lacking classic symptoms. Clinical Descriptions Paroxysms of Cough: Frequent, spasmodic bursts of 5–10 coughs during a single expiration, often accompanied by bulging eyes, protruding tongue, cyanosis, and visible neck vein distension. Episodes are worse at night and disrupt sleep. Whoop: A characteristic sound produced by rapid inspiration against a closed glottis at the end of a coughing fit. Post-Tussive Vomiting: Vomiting immediately after coughing, sometimes expelling a mucus plug. Exclusion of Other Causes: Chronic cough causes like tuberculosis, asthma, and chronic bronchitis must be ruled out. Associated Signs and Symptoms Pertussis can cause complications due to increased intrathoracic pressure during coughing fits, including: Subconjunctival and intracranial hemorrhages. Rectal prolapse. Hernias. Pneumothorax. Petechiae. Rib fractures. Response to Suspected Cases Within 24 Hours: The clinician must notify public health authorities. Within 48 Hours: Public health authorities should investigate the case, including: Completing a case investigation form. Collecting two nasopharyngeal swabs before initiating treatment (treatment should not be delayed for lab results). Conducting laboratory tests. Confirming and classifying the case. Close contacts should be identified, and symptomatic contacts should receive treatment. Active case searches should be conducted. Specimen Collection Nasopharyngeal Swabs: Collect within four weeks of cough onset. Two swabs are ideal—one for culture and one for PCR testing. Use sterile polyester, rayon, or nylon flocked swabs (not cotton). Avoid throat and anterior nasal swabs. Culture: Specimens should be plated on selective media (e.g., Regan–Lowe agar) or placed in transport media and sent to the lab within 24 hours. PCR Testing: Specimens should be placed in sterile tubes or transport media. If only one swab is available, it should be placed in Regan–Lowe transport media. Serology: Conducted 4–12 weeks after cough onset, using serum samples for IgG anti-pertussis toxin antibody testing. Avoid serology in children ≤10 years or recently vaccinated individuals due to low sensitivity and interference from vaccine-induced antibodies. Laboratory Testing Culture: The gold standard for confirming pertussis, though it is relatively insensitive (<60%). Success rates are highest in infants and decrease with prior antibiotic use, delayed specimen collection, or vaccination. PCR: More sensitive and rapid than culture but prone to false positives (due to cross-contamination) and false negatives (with delayed testing or antibiotic use). PCR assays vary across laboratories, and no standardized protocols exist. Serology: Useful for retrospective diagnosis in adolescents and adults but not recommended for children ≤10 years or recently vaccinated individuals. This document provides a detailed framework for pertussis surveillance, emphasizing the importance of timely case detection, specimen collection, and laboratory testing to inform public health strategies and improve disease control.
